I once assumed the Grand Incense Rite resembled festivals in other nations: cultural practices that grew out of commemoration and sacrifice, preserving certain customs as tradition. Ordinarily, such customs become simpler and more secularised as time advances.

Yet after examining every extant record of the Rite within Huaxu, I found that its central custom — the act of incense offering itself — has remained unchanged in both materials and quantity for nearly a thousand years of recorded history.

Given the manifest presence of "divine" power within Huaxu's territory, I have reason to believe the Rite is not merely a cultural or political form of worship. It may have a distinct functional purpose. Put plainly: in Huaxu, and only in Huaxu, a rite that exchanges offerings for a deity's protection appears to function as an actual transaction.

But why would Taihao require these incenses? And what, in fact, is Taihao? No comparable records exist elsewhere in Atlasia, and the incense used for such offerings is produced only within Huaxu... Incense found only here — and a "god" found only here that feeds upon it? The symmetry is too neat. It feels less like coincidence than design.

...

This functional reading suggests an intriguing possibility. Perhaps Huaxu's so-called "divinities" are not the exalted beings of popular imagination at all, but something closer to a machine — an apparatus that regulates the environment within its sphere of influence. It may even affect, or outright control, nearby Filthoids, pressing them into service as a blunt tool of enforcement. In that case, the Grand Incense Rite is less a ceremony than a scheduled procedure: refuelling this immense "machine" with what Huaxu calls "incense", at fixed intervals and in fixed amounts.

If this conjecture proves true, it would imply that, a thousand years ago, the people of Huaxu had mastered a technology capable of creating a "god". Should such a technology be deciphered, the Nine Chapters of Dafeng might be extended across Atlasia; or the mechanism's field of influence might be scaled down to the individual, enabling the creation of specialised protective devices.

Yet if such a technology truly exists, why does it function only within Huaxu's borders? Even the Starweavers have left no record of employing similar techniques beyond Huaxu’s border. What, then, is the crucial factor that imposes this limitation?

...

name: Qing's Wish
desc:
A tale of Yin Qing, a poet of ancient Huaxu, drawn from Bygone Fragments, an essay collection by the later author Cang Xian. In it, a young traveller known only as Feng — his family name now lost to history — drifts into Haojing and discovers a green leaf inscribed with a poem drifting along a waterway beside the Yin residence — a small happenstance that binds their fates.

preserves a number of literary anecdotes from roughly five centuries past, steeped in the flavour of legend. Its reliability as a historical source remains open to question, yet its value as literature is widely acknowledged.
desc2:
...

The leaf had long since turned yellow, yet the traces of ink upon it remained clear. Yin Qing studied it, gave a long, wistful sigh, and after a moment allowed himself a faint smile.
"I once wished to roam the world," he said to Feng, "yet my father and mother would not permit it. So I wrote upon this green leaf and set it adrift with the current, to ease my longing. Now that you have chanced upon it, carry it with you on your travels, that my wish may journey beside you."
Feng was silent for a long while. Then he replied,
"Why should we not travel together?"

...

When they reached the Lin River, Feng was stricken with a grave illness and lay bedridden. Qing said, "Rest now, and recover your strength. I shall remain here until you are well; then we shall set out again."
But Feng would not agree. He drew forth the withered leaf and pressed it into Qing's hand.
"Take this leaf," he said. "Go far. Let it be as though we still travel side by side."

...

Qing travelled far and wide, and in time he filled an entire chest with his verses. Wherever he went, he won admirers who pressed him to remain, yet he declined them all.
In his later years, he returned once more to the familiar banks of the Lin. Before Feng's grave, he buried the withered leaf in the soil and laid fresh green leaves above it.
Upon a leaf he inscribed two lines:

"Green leaves lie upon your grave;
The ache in my heart drifts with the stream."

name: Footsteps Across Huaxu – Haojing
desc: An excerpt from Xu Xingke's Footsteps Across Huaxu, an officially commissioned travelogue. In it, Xu sets down his impressions of his homeland — its regions, its people, and the ideas they awaken.
desc2:
Hall of Adjudication

In the early days of the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, the Hall of Adjudication played a far more prominent role. Its original purpose, however, has long since faded from common memory and is now known only to a handful of dedicated historians.

Beneath the Hall, a bridge-like span arches across the air like a rainbow. Legend holds that Lord Argent sometimes soars through the heavens and listens, unmoving, to the clamour of the mortal world — proof that Heaven heeds the people, and that divine law watches over all.

Today, the Hall stands as Huaxu's political centre. It rises against the clouds, visible from nearly anywhere in Haojing — much as the Nine Chapters of Dafeng stand before the people: clear, enduring, and impossible to ignore.

⸻

Zesheng Pharmacy

In former times, the people of Huaxu turned to healers of the Zhuyou clan when illness struck. In later ages, physicians devoted to pharmacology emerged, along with apothecaries to prepare and dispense medicines.

Zesheng Pharmacy is Haojing's most respected establishment of its kind. It is said that its founder was once herself a Zhuyou, yet she abandoned those arts in favour of pharmacology, elevating the discipline to new heights. Rare herbs and medicinal ingredients are supplied here, and the pharmacy is renowned for its proprietary prescriptions. It also offers seasonal wellness regimens to help preserve one's health.

If thirst overtakes you while wandering the streets, do stop by — herbal tonics are served free to the public.

⸻

Youlai Alley

Some popular Huaxu tales claim that the dead may linger in a form known as Wishen. Unlike the fearful portrayals of spirits and ghosts found in other lands, Huaxu's Wishen are remembered in legend as gentle, even endearing beings. Though they may occasionally cause minor disturbances, it is often out of kindness, as if to guide the living along their path.

Haojing folklore speaks of a place called Youlai Alley, where Wishen with unfinished attachments are said to gather. Most dismiss such claims as idle fancy. Yet there are whispers that if one follows the winding lanes of the eastern quarter long enough, one might, by chance, stumble into that mysterious domain...

⸻

Jiaolan Village

If Haojing's bustle begins to wear on you, head west. Jiaolan Village offers a quiet refuge from the city's noise. This small settlement lies on Haojing's western outskirts, close enough to reach on foot.

Huaxu's incense culture stretches back into antiquity, and Jiaolan Village is regarded as its birthplace. Though the craft of incense-making has long since spread across the land, and Jiaolan is no longer the only place to find it, it remains home to the largest incense-drying grounds in the region surrounding Haojing. When the aromatic plants come into bloom, villagers harvest them, rinse them clean, and lay them out beneath the sun. On fair days, when a gentle breeze passes through, the fragrance carries for miles, creating an atmosphere at once ethereal and intoxicating.

Before you depart, should you wish to bring home a thoughtful gift, the villagers' handcrafted incense makes an excellent choice: elegant in scent, and rich in Huaxu's distinctive cultural character.

name: Huaxu Trends – Haojing Special
desc:
Huaxu Trends tracks what's trending across Huaxu: new places to eat and drink, clothing and everyday essentials, and lifestyles arriving from overseas and taking hold at home.
Each year, the Haojing Special drops a month before the Grand Incense Rite, spotlighting the capital's latest go-to spots for food, leisure, and nightlife.
desc2:
Top Dining Pick: Bazhen Pavilion

In last month's reader poll, Bazhen Pavilion beat the runner-up by nearly a hundred votes — clearly a crowd favourite.

Our rule is simple: we don't recommend what we haven't tried. So we went in as ordinary diners and ordered the signature dishes. The fan-favourite Bazhen Tofu really is a standout: silky-soft, layered with flavour, and finished with a scatter of corn kernels — looks as good as it tastes.

Mistwharf Vinegar Fish is a classic, but the sharp vinegar tang isn't for everyone, especially with freshwater fish. A couple of us left it unfinished.

...

From Diner A: Chef Bai's cooking speaks for itself. And Chef Li isn't far behind. Word is his poems are just as good as his food.

From Diner B: When I was young, my family always celebrated my birthday at Bazhen Pavilion... Years have gone by. Though the people who once sat beside me are no longer with me, the dishes taste the same. And perhaps that is enough.

From Diner C: Whenever friends or relatives visit Haojing, Bazhen Pavilion is the first place I take them. That said, lately some of the new dishes feel like they're trying a little too hard to please out-of-towners. It's not quite the same as it used to be — not that there's anything wrong with catering to visitors.

...

name: Ode to the Nine Chapters
desc:
A short piece praising the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, written in Huaxu's distinctive panegyric style.
From the wording and the marginal note appended below, the author appears to be a student still learning the craft of writing.

name: A Compendium of Incense
desc: A celebrated Huaxu classic, reputedly written by a master of Xuanheng Sect. The work runs to seventeen volumes, with additions made by later generations. The excerpt below is drawn from the book's preface.
desc2:
The art of incense has changed with the ages. In antiquity, aromatic herbs were burnt to raise fragrant smoke to reach the divine; in the present age, incense is measured and its vapours harmonised, so that by this craft the Mandate of Heaven may be set in order.

The Record of Yang's Life relates that at the founding of the Nine Chapters, Yang declared: "When the Mandate of Heaven intermingles, all courses are impeded, and what is tangled cannot easily be loosed." She therefore sent men to gather a myriad of aromatics and heap them at the Taixu Mausoleum, where they were burnt without cease, day and night. Yang herself sat beside the pyre. When the smoke ran thick, none could draw near; and when at last it thinned, she had vanished.

This account need not be taken on faith. Versions differ from place to place, and much has shifted with the passing of years. I compile this book not to quarrel over such tales, but to set down the incense arts of Huaxu across the span of ages. Within these pages I have gathered, as exhaustively as I could, matters of Heaven and Earth, of human affairs and the produce of the land; what was ancient is collected, and what is current is brought within its compass. It is my hope that those who come after may follow this lineage, and enrich it in their turn.

The whole consists of seventeen volumes. The first nine record the incense materials: orchid and fragrant herb, pepper and cassia, aloeswood, sandalwood, borneol and musk — ancient varieties of Huaxu — together with rare foreign aromatics once presented as tribute.

Marginal note: Since the widening of the Starweavers' routes, what was once unheard-of has become obtainable.

The next four volumes treat of the uses of incense. Incense serves many ends: for offering, for wear, and for medicine. These are set out in detail below.

The final three volumes concern the art of incense blending. Though its principles may appear simple, it is in truth the most demanding of all related crafts. One must first master the preceding thirteen volumes and commit them thoroughly to memory; only then may one properly undertake this discipline.

The uses of incense are as boundless as the sea, and their subtleties are still beyond our full grasp. I have done no more than gather and preserve a handful of remarkable formulae devised by sages of old, that their methods might endure.

name: A Match Made
desc: A folk opera script popular among Huaxu's commoners. It follows a young couple from first meeting to marriage, only for petty quarrels and everyday slights to sour things afterwards. Said to be adapted from a real case in Haojing, though this cannot be verified. Excerpt follows.
desc2:
No need for the Moon Matchmaker to meddle. One red thread binds the romance. The crimson bridal sedan chair halts at the gate. Whether she wills it or no — gown on, veil down — once she mounts, the union is sealed. A hundred hands bear it onwards. The bridegroom reels, heart unmoored, as though he had glimpsed a heavenly maiden in a dream.

(Offstage, a hurried reply.)
Jing (beaming): Splendid! Good luck upon good luck — three cups for that!
Mo: It's late. My lady is waiting. I'll be taking my leave.
Jing: Nonsense! You've drained more cups than I can count at the Bazhen Pavilion and never once been drunk. And now you're baulking at a single cup? You'll be the laughingstock!
Mo: Things aren't what they were. Don't take it amiss, brother.
(Mo bows with clasped hands.)
Jing (laughing): Ha! And here I thought you were a man of mettle — turns out you go to ground the moment wine's poured.
Jing: Fine, fine. If he's that set on ducking out, no need to push it.
Mo (startled): Why would you say that? All these years of brotherhood, and you'd throw it away over one cup of wine?
Jing: Brotherhood? If that means anything to you — today's your wedding day, everyone's here to toast you. And you won't drink a single cup with us?
All: Hear, hear!
Jing: Some loyalty. Some brother.
All: Hear, hear!
Mo (sighing): Pomegranate blazes red as fire... and still, it cannot match the bitter smoke of mugwort... Ah, well.
Mo (raising his voice): Today I'll drink with you if it kills me. Gentlemen — your health!
(All drink.)

A crescent moon crests the little tower, yet its tender light falls only into the gutter. Hair dressed in vain, pipa in hand... whose ear awaits her song?

name: Inventive Sachets: Notes from My Workbench
desc:
A young artisan's personal notes, loosely recording a few ways to make scented sachets.
It isn't a proper how-to, and the steps aren't laid out in full. Best enjoyed as a casual read.
desc2:
A sachet to cheer up my workaholic friends
— 1 part Ivorywood, 3 parts Vernal Prime.
Vernal Prime has a crisp, refreshing fragrance, perfect for a more "put-together" vibe. Ivorywood helps keep you steady when work gets stressful.

A sachet to win the hearts of every stray cat
— A small pinch of Loong Qiqi, 4 parts Ivorywood.
The secret is that tiny salty, fishy note in Loong Qiqi — it smells a little wild, in a way cats seem to love. Add the cosy warmth of Ivorywood, and they might just decide we're "one of them".

A sachet to help my favourite author update faster
— As much Frostleaf as you can manage.
Frostleaf keeps you wide awake, so the writer I'm following can pull an all-nighter and get a chapter out. So yes: be generous... Teehee...

name: Hall of Craft Annual Record: Works Digest
desc: A substantial volume detailing the Ministry of Works' most recent public projects.
desc2:
The Ministry of Works hereby announces the following works under its charge:

Ⅰ. Rehabilitation of Official Roads
By order, the city's principal roads and minor roads are to be repaired and reinforced. Roadbeds shall be strengthened and carriageways widened, easing the passage of carts and riders and improving travel throughout the city, so that the routes may run clear in all directions.

Ⅱ. Construction of Freight-Handling Apparatus
New freight-handling apparatus shall be constructed, with a wrought-iron frame and precision gearing. Efficiency shall be improved and operations standardised, speeding the circulation of goods and encouraging commercial growth.

Ⅲ. Reinforcement and Repair of the Wharves
The existing wharves shall undergo full inspection and repair. Riverbanks shall be reinforced, rotted timbers replaced, and additional safeguards installed, ensuring safe passage for vessels and keeping grain transport secure.

...

All works shall be carried out in accordance with established codes: rooted in traditional practice, yet open to new techniques. The Ministry of Works faithfully discharges its duty, securing the foundations of the state and serving the needs of the people.

Those wishing to consult the full project files may do so in the Ministry's archives.

name: The Sayings of Master Zhuxi
desc: A record of Master Zhuxi's sayings, written down by his students. His views shifted with age, yet his words were preserved throughout his life, from his earliest years to his last. Excerpt follows.
desc2:
In considering what the sages of old intended when they taught learning, I take it to be this: to press inquiry to its limits, and to read widely in the old and the new, so as to broaden the mind and enlarge one's view. Only then may a person judge right from wrong, weigh matters with clarity, and grasp the workings of the world — not merely memorise texts and polish fine phrases for the sake of fame, profit, and preferment.

Those who study in our day have borne hardships for too long. Much of what the former worthies taught is recorded in the classics, yet remains detached from worldly affairs. Anyone with resolve ought to read deeply, reflect, and question — to examine and sift what one has learned. For if one recognises the vastness of Heaven and Earth and the complexity of affairs, and strives to look upon all things with objectivity and a mind trained to weigh matters with discernment, then the standards by which one stands in the world and conducts oneself are already within one's grasp. Why wait for others to hand them over before one can hold fast to them?

As for what I have written, it cannot guide every student, and the methods it proposes may not fully accord with the true aim of opening the mind and awakening thought. Therefore I shall no longer require it in this hall. Instead, I have selected the main principles by which the sages taught learning, set them forth as articles, and posted them here for all to see. Let all of you study them together, make their meaning clear, keep them, and hold yourselves to them. Then, in the midst of your thoughts and actions, your judgement will grow more exacting: you will deliberate with care, discern with clarity, and investigate things so as to extend your knowledge. These are, in truth, the roots of conduct in the world, and the foundations of cultivating virtue and turning towards the good.

Only by keeping to this guiding framework may one contemplate all things, and so bring forth new understanding and open new paths.

name: Training Yard Booking Log
desc:
Most fresh faces in Outer Peaks get told the same thing on their first day: "Done with your errands? Go take a look at the training yard."
It was originally set up so the Drifters could spar and hone their craft, but over time, it has picked up a few... additional uses.
desc2:
4 June
Filed by: Wang Quan
Reason: I say sweet tofu pudding is best. Zhang Fu swears by the savoury kind. Only one way to settle it — a match!

28 June
Filed by: Xu Hong
Reason: I want to test a new explosive prototype. The yard is open enough for it.

15 July
Filed by: Su Yi
Reason: Lu Ye and Pei Jing want to practise with crossbows. I've been asked to keep an eye on them.

16 July
Filed by: Su Yi
Reason: Same as yesterday (the kids are really coming along!).

6 August
Filed by: Uncle Tang
Reason: Finished a new battlefield loudhailer. Need everyone to take turns singing in the yard for a sound test.

20 August
Filed by: Uncle Tang
Reason: Zhu Pu overtrained and hurt his leg. Want to test the support brace I made for him and log a few measurements.

name: Workshop Experiment Log
desc: A workshop logbook where Outer Peaks' artisans jot down their wild ideas and odd contraptions. In the name of "learning from one another", Uncle Tang later insisted on adding a comment board so everyone could leave their thoughts underneath.
desc2:
I. Meowvellous Machine

Logged by: Uncle Tang (love you lot, everyone in Outer Peaks!)

Setup:
Split the kids into two groups. One got a pep talk from the Meowvellous Machine beforehand; the other didn't.
Both groups then read Mechanism Basics That Every Huaxu Kid Can Learn. After one stick of incense, we gave them a quiz.

Result:
Some of the "encouraged" kids (Zhu Pu, for instance) made the top ten. Others landed near the bottom. The kids who didn't get the pep talk (like Pei Jing) ended up somewhere in the middle.

Comments:
Su Yi: The groups weren't evenly matched to begin with. The results don't prove anything.
Xu Hong: I think some of them were just scared by how the machine looks.
Kezhou: The results aren't the point. I just want to ask... what's with that signature in the "Logged by" line? Has Uncle Tang been breathing in workshop fumes again?


II. Duck and Dash

Logged by: Uncle Tang (still loving you lot today)

Setup:
After basic safety checks, we went out into the wild. On spotting a lone Sable Bi'an, give a Duck and Dash a full wind and toss it.

Result:
Didn't scare it off. If anything, it made so much noise that it drew more of them in and made them meaner.

Areas to Improve:
Try making it even louder.

Comments:
Su Yi: Why not pack it with a few small charges? Like the firecrackers we set off at New Year — toss it, then leg it while it's popping.
Uncle Tang: This is meant for schoolchildren to use for self-defence on the way home. If we add anything like that, I'm worried they'll misuse it and hurt themselves.
Shen Han: Are the children all right? No one was hurt, I hope? Uncle Tang — please don't drag them into such dangerous experiments next time!

name: The Incense Trial: The Civil Service Exam in Smoke and Scent
desc: An anonymous miscellany from Huaxu, offering a detailed account of the rules and procedures of the Incense Trial.
desc2:
Within Huaxu's system of governance, few institutions are as distinctive as the Incense Trial — an annual examination established by the Ministry of Rites to seek out promising talent among the young. Built around Huaxu's own incense culture, it proceeds in stages, each stricter than the last. Learning is tested openly; character and suitability are weighed more quietly. In time, it has become a signature feature of Huaxu's governance.

Shrine Trial — Timed by Smoke, Judged by Learning
The selection begins with the Shrine Trial, a small regional examination held throughout Huaxu. Each sitting is held at the district's Argent Loong Temple: a first-round screening, and a gesture of reverence to Lord Argent. The trial is conducted inside the temple itself, overseen by the temple's incense wardens, who are charged with keeping order and impartiality from start to finish.
There is no interview at this stage; the focus is purely on a candidate's learning. On the appointed day, candidates enter with their admission slips and take their seats. Writing materials are issued, but no one may touch brush to paper until permitted. Only when the supervising warden lights the designated Lunarose incense, and the candidates have completed their rite of thanks to Lord Argent, does the examination begin in earnest. The time allowed is exactly the burn of a single stick of Lunarose incense.
The top three from each sitting advance, and must in due course travel to Huaxu's capital, Haojing, for a harsher round of selection.

Departmental Trial — Matched to Post, Weighed in Talent and Virtue
Candidates who reach Haojing then face the Departmental Trial, where suitability is the core concern. Unlike the Shrine Trial, which leans on written testing, this stage is not centred on the brush alone. Greater weight is placed on practical ability and how well a candidate fits the duties of the post. Interviews allow examiners to judge a candidate's speech, thinking, and character at closer range. Before sitting the trial, candidates must state their intended post, making an initial choice among the Three Ministries and their subordinate departments. The assessment shifts accordingly, depending on the functions of the chosen institution.
The close of the Departmental Trial marks the end of that year's Incense Trial. Once the list of successful candidates is confirmed, the Ministry of Rites summons all qualified entrants to the Hall of Adjudication to take up their appointments. Those whose talent and conduct are deemed exceptional may even win the favour of Lord Argent. In such cases, a Bi'an delivers a summons, granting leave to advance to a third stage: a final selection for the office of High Chancellor of Loongyuan.
During this interval, the Hall of Adjudication enters a brief recess to prepare postings and the High Chancellor selection to follow. Meanwhile, the Hall of Incense hastens its own preparations, assembling special aromatics reserved solely for the High Chancellor's selection.

As for how the High Chancellor of Loongyuan is ultimately chosen — Huaxu has no shortage of opinions. I have only learned that an internal procedure does exist, and that it is said to be fairly comprehensive.
For reasons of space, however, we'll leave Loongyuan for the next issue.

name: How to Become High Chancellor of Loongyuan
desc: A tongue-in-cheek essay that claims to explain how to become High Chancellor of Loongyuan. So exaggerated and irreverent that it's hard to tell where fact ends and invention begins.
desc2:
Do you want to become High Chancellor of Loongyuan?
Let me be specific: set aside the tangled official duties the post entails. Imagine instead that you keep the title and bask in universal admiration across Huaxu without having to lift a finger. Under those conditions, do you want it?
I expect most answers would be: of course!
Which brings us to the real question: how does one actually become High Chancellor of Loongyuan?

In last issue, we touched on the Incense Trial — the examination system by which the state selects officials from among the common run of Huaxu's citizens. But what of those so-called prodigies, the dazzling geniuses beyond the common measure? Is there a special track reserved for them? Are they appointed the moment they first wail into the world?
Certainly not.
Becoming High Chancellor of Loongyuan is no simple matter. Most readers will have guessed correctly: those singled out do indeed receive a message from Lord Argent — delivered, of course, by a Bi'an. But don't celebrate just yet. Receiving the message does not mean you've already made it. All it gives you is a new label: Candidate for High Chancellor of Loongyuan.
You answer the summons and travel to Haojing. There, the sitting High Chancellor receives you with great warmth. You gather in the Hall of Adjudication and talk — perhaps of state affairs, perhaps simply of daily life. This stage has a name: "The Trial of the Way."
When it ends, you are escorted back to your temporary quarters at the posting station to await the next summons.
And you wait.
Days pass. You pace like a cat on a hot tin roof, opening the door every few moments to see whether someone has come with news. The good news is that someone eventually does. If they didn't, this essay would end here — and then what would you do with your evening?

Filled with anticipation, you return once more to the Hall of Adjudication. You assume that since your previous examiner was the sitting High Chancellor of Loongyuan, this time you must surely meet Lord Argent themselves. But upon arrival, you notice there is no Lord Argent, nor the High Chancellor. Instead, a handful of Hall staffers hurriedly thrust an enormous stack of dossiers into your arms and then flee at once, as if the building is about to collapse.
Now comes your task: in this sea of records, you must trace the links between designated incidents and present your own reasoned conclusions. Someone will see to your meals, your lodging, your daily needs. You, however, are strictly forbidden from cutting corners. Try to slack off and you will be struck from the candidate list without ceremony.
This stage is called "The Trial of Statecraft."
Naturally, you are exceptional. After what feels like years poring over records — memorising every last petty detail from the past twenty years — you finally receive word one morning: you passed. The Trial of Statecraft is complete. Next comes, supposedly, an audience with Lord Argent.
You are beside yourself. You rush to Qianxiu Pavilion to have a new set of robes made — something bright and showy for the occasion. How many people go their entire lives without hearing even a single true word from Lord Argent? And you — you might see Them with your own eyes. What fortune beyond measure!
Unable to contain your excitement, you tell the shop assistant exactly why you are having clothes made. The girl takes one look at your glowing face and cannot help it: she covers her mouth and giggles.
"You know," she says, "not every candidate gets to see Lord Argent."
You go pale. You are just about to seek a further explanation when a messenger arrives with urgent orders: report to the Hall of Adjudication at once and prepare for the Trial of the Heart. With no time to dig, you hurriedly straighten your robes and make your way back to that now-familiar place.

Inside, incense smoke curls through the Hall — thick enough to be seen, yet without the faintest scent. This seems odd. An attendant arrives and has you sit on a cushion with the other candidates, instructing you to meditate and regulate your breath. Suspicious but obedient, you sit. Smoke coils around your eyes and nose. Your thoughts grow heavy. Drowsiness steals over you. You think you might as well close your eyes for a moment. So you do.
And you fall asleep.
You dream a long dream.
In it, you see your past: your mother cradling you, your father lifting you high above his head.
In it, you see your future: you succeed to the post of High Chancellor of Loongyuan, spend a lifetime wringing yourself dry for the people of Huaxu, and at last are laid to rest in the Taixu Mausoleum.
In it, you see others — countless faces, countless eyes fixed upon you. Questions rise, one after another, pressing and demanding. You are flustered, drenched in sweat, pushed to the brink — and then you jolt awake.
You look up. The incense lit at the beginning has not yet burned out.

In the end, you do not pass the selection. Presumably, your performance in the dream failed to please Lord Argent. Still, though not chosen, you ultimately join the Hall of Incense and continue serving the people of Huaxu. A happy ending all the same, wouldn't you say?

And so, dear readers, you now know exactly how to become High Chancellor of Loongyuan. And if one of you actually does make it to High Chancellor someday... well, I trust you'll remember me, the humble author who wrote this helpful little piece. A little token of appreciation sent my way would not go amiss. Don't you think?

name: Dawn of Haojing — Issue Ⅰ
desc: A daily paper printed by the Hall of Craft and sold on the streets of Haojing. Mostly local happenings and the occasional public notice. Truth be told, it has never had many readers.
desc2:
Ⅰ. East Market: Floodwater Half-Drowns a Lord Argent Statue

After days of relentless rain, Haojing Lake rose fast enough to spill over the East Market embankment. One shopkeeper, known locally for his devotion, kept a three-foot wooden statue of Lord Argent at his shopfront and burnt incense to it each day without fail.
Early one morning, a shophand named Zhang opened up the shop to sweep the threshold — only to find the water already lapping at the steps, the statue's lower half swallowed up. Startled, Zhang shouted for help, and the neighbours together hauled the image further inside.
Tongues wag: "Lord Argent's ways are inscrutable." Surely this is Their doing — making plain Their displeasure at private offerings by flooding Their own image, a stark reminder to respect the seasons and Heaven's will.


Ⅱ. Astonishing: Sixty-Two-Year-Old Widow Gives Birth

Mrs Liu of Haojing, a widow of sixty-two, has long lived alone and childless, and in her quiet days was often lonely.
In recent months, she complained frequently of fatigue and found her appetite greatly increased. Neighbours took it for the usual signs of age. No one expected what came after: on the nineteenth of this month, she gave birth to a baby boy — loud-voiced when he cried, bright-eyed, and fine-featured.
Word soon reached the Hall of Founts, which sent an officer to verify the matter. Mrs Liu claims that three months ago she dreamt of a woman in blue who offered her a peach, sweet beyond telling; upon waking, she felt her body begin to change. The child bears a faint red birthmark at the waist, shaped unmistakably like a peach — proof that the dream was no mere fancy.
Strange indeed. Such tales belong, people say, to storybooks — not to everyday life. The neighbours insist Mrs Liu has always been known for kindness, and some whisper that Heaven, in its own way, repays the virtuous.
The Hall of Founts has registered the child and granted assistance in grain and bolts of cloth. Friends and relations arrive daily with congratulations, and curious onlookers have been gathering in no small numbers.


Ⅲ. West Market Oddity: A Dog That Hunts Rats

At the West Market eatery Baiwei House, the proprietor Li Sanlang keeps a yellow dog named Rusty to mind the place at night. He has been a good dog: quiet, steady, and has never caused trouble.
On the afternoon of the first of this month, the shophands were airing out dried ingredients in the sun when Rusty suddenly wouldn't stop barking. They hurried over and saw him dart to a rat hole at the base of the wall. A moment later he came back out with a grey rat clenched in his jaws, already dead.
Taken aback, the hands reported it to Li Sanlang. Li wouldn't believe a word of it — until the next day, when he saw it with his own eyes: Rusty crouched by the hole, and the moment a rat poked its head out, he lunged. Before the day was out, he'd caught three. One regular laughed: "The old saying compares a dog that catches mice to nosy folk who meddle in other people's business — but it's a blessing when your place is full of rats."
Since then, Rusty has hunted rats by day and kept watch by night. Baiwei House, it is said, has had no trouble with rats since.

name: Dawn of Haojing — Issue Ⅱ
desc: A daily paper printed by the Hall of Craft and sold on the streets of Haojing. Mostly local happenings and the occasional public notice. Truth be told, it has never had many readers.
desc2:
(The sheet has been trampled and scuffed; much of the text is blurred.)
...

Ⅱ. Unrest on the Western Outskirts — Drifters Sighted Again?

In recent days, citizens have been arriving at the Ministry of Fortune in growing numbers, reporting that along the back paths of the western outskirts, shadowy figures have been seen lingering. Those who claim to have spoken with them describe shifty replies and evasive eyes — hardly the bearing of decent folk. It is feared some mischief is being plotted in secret.
Though Huaxu stands under the protection of the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, Drifters have long been said to lurk even within Haojing, committing offence upon offence. A censer that had burned unbroken for a hundred years was once extinguished — doused with water by the most notorious of their lot. Another drove a mechapuppet straight into the Hall of Adjudication. Others have hung wenzhu fronds outside people's doors to mark their targets, then ambushed them and left them bleeding. Their crimes are many; their wickedness unrepentant.
Even so, there are always those who make excuses for them, shielding them in the dark and dressing them up with fine names like the Four Drifters. Fortunately, the Magistrates of Yingtian took action, and the so-called Four Drifters were seized and put to death.
Yet though their ringleaders and close followers have been dealt with, remnants are said to remain. The people fear renewed Drifter activity may flare again and bring fresh calamity.
The Hall of Adjudication has therefore issued the following order: the Magistrates' patrols are to be strengthened at once. A reward of 12,000 is hereby offered for any report of Drifters' whereabouts that is verified. Residents are further warned: do not enter desolate places after nightfall. Every measure is to be taken to root out the Drifters.
...
...
...
 (The latter half of the sheet is torn; the remaining text is illegible.)

name: Notes on the Mirage (Ⅱ)
desc: A book set down by a man of letters surnamed Shen. Its authenticity cannot be verified, but it remains an entertaining read. Much of the text has been lost to time. This is Part Ⅱ.
desc2:
On the surface of Haojing Lake, mist sometimes gathers into shapes — towers, palaces, immortals, spectres — each outlined with startling clarity. People call such sights the Mirage. Some say it is Lord Argent's breath; others insist it is the work of Lord Argent's eight immortal attendants. Accounts multiply without end. I doubt them all.

I chased down every rumour I could find, yet reached no firm conclusion. I went about the city seeking out the elders, asking how one might reach the Mirage, and I began with the boatmen, hoping they would row me across the lake in search of it. They mocked my folly — yet they agreed readily once paid, and accompanied me on several trips. Back and forth we went, again and again, and still we found nothing.

I searched daily until my meagre means were spent. A few, taking pity, would join me in their spare hours, though their earlier enthusiasm was gone. I did not resent them; I felt only shame. In the end I put what little remained to my name into buying a bamboo raft, resolved to seek the Mirage on my own.

Though I am but a bookish sort, I grew up climbing hills and swimming rivers with the neighbourhood boys. I am no weakling — yet my skills go no further than that. At first, poling the raft was awkward and stiff; with time I grew steadily more practised.

The search proved arduous indeed. At first I tried to take my bearings and fix a heading. Later there was only the endless expanse, drifting and bobbing with the waves. Still I never beheld the Mirage's true face. In time my spirit faltered. I began to suspect I was clinging to emptiness, wasting my days and wearing down my resolve. Now and then I would glimpse it in the distance and strain towards it, only for it to vanish the moment I drew near — like moonlight on water, dissolving into nothing at the slightest touch.

One day a thick fog rolled in over Haojing, and I could not make out a person two steps away. Everyone warned me not to go, fearing I would lose my way on the lake and die there. I sighed and said, "Other than my life, what do I have left to lose?" My purse was already empty. We scraped by on my wife's needlework. Thankfully we had no children; otherwise, what kind of husband would that make me?

Still I insisted on leaving. My wife wept and tried to stop me. "If you step out that door," she said, "I will never be your wife again." My resolve faltered — yet in the end I steeled myself, flung the door wide, and went.

The fog blotted out heaven and earth. When the tip of my pole struck the water, I could not even see where it fell. I could only feel the raft's motion through my wrists. The cold was sharper than on any ordinary day; it cut to the bone. Frost gathered in my beard; I breathed it away, and moments later it formed again.

Nothing about the scene seemed especially strange. Perhaps there was something wondrous, yet my mind was so muddled that I could not recall it. I remember only one instant: at one point it felt as though my pole was no longer meeting water at all, but something lighter — like pushing through cloud. A feeling too surreal for words to depict.

I cannot say how long I went on. Then the fog began to thin. Before me, overlapping haloes of light shimmered, and within them rose halls and pavilions, radiant beyond measure. Joy seized me like a fever. I gathered what strength remained and drove the raft forward. Just as my strength drained, the raft struck shore. It was as though a stone had finally dropped from my chest. My heart, at last, began to steady.

I left the raft behind and stepped ashore. The ground beneath my feet felt soft as water, yet I neither sank nor grew wet. With each step, ripples spread outward. It was wonder that defied belief.

...

name: A Box of Paper Stars
desc: A box of paper stars crafted from expired tickets. It's said that a certain number of these can bless one's wishes and dreams, though this seems not to be the case.

name: A Girl's Old Clothes
desc: A piece of worn clothing, hiding a palm-sized diary within its thin lining. The name "Alice" is legible on the cover, but most entries are lost to stains, with only recent scribbles faintly recognisable.

name: Treasure on the Saddle
desc: A worn adventure novel depicting the protagonist and his lean horse conquering a castle to find treasure.

name: Familiar Wire Portrait
desc: A wire sculpture of Berenica in profile, skillfully capturing her defining features.

name: Medical Kit
desc: A standard-issue medical kit used by the Legion. It contains the essentials for treating minor battlefield injuries, but offers little help for more severe trauma.

name: Avar's Photograph
desc: A cherished keepsake Avar always carries, showing him with his daughter Daphne as a child. Though yellowed with age, their bright smiles remain unmistakable.

name: Bloodstained Photograph
desc: Once a cherished keepsake Avar carried with him, featuring a blissful moment of him with his daughter Daphne as a child. Now, their bright smiles are smeared by dark, dried bloodstains.

name: White Flower
desc: A flower given to you by Psyche, with the warmth of her touch still lingering on the stem.

name: A Dangerous Prescription
desc: A seemingly simple prescription that conceals a dangerous secret — seditious text hidden on the back. If ever discovered by Imperial eyes, it could spell disaster.

name: Portrait Gift from Faye
desc: An abstract portrait gifted to you by Faye, who insists it's your likeness. The interplay of red and white might vaguely suggest a human form, gender indistinguishable, but if Faye sees you in it, then so be it. Perhaps the aesthetic sensibilities of Inner City denizens are an acquired taste.

name: Old Key
desc: An intricately crafted key, oddly familiar yet unplaceable. Its origin remains elusive, but perhaps one day, at the right moment, it will unlock a long-buried secret.

name: Weaponholder
desc: A widely used auxiliary bracket equipped with various clasps for a stable structure, allowing craftsmen to fix weapons on it for adjustment.
desc2:
"Few know that the Gad Weaponholder was the first patented invention. When the patent system was first introduced, no one was willing to risk their trade secrets; while the Gad Weaponholder is simple in technology, so it was put forward to test the waters. Of course, it ended up being a tremendous success. Ol' Gad could have made a fortune from this patent, but, 'I've made a mere holder ace all my life. I'm just glad you all like it. Go ahead, use it as you wish, for free!' said he. Quite touching, isn't it?"

— Dylan the Walking Encyclopedia, in "Into the Unseen Corners"

name: Flamme De Epuration: Bolt
desc: Crafted with precision from the blueprint of Flamme De Epuration. There is no turning back once the trigger is pulled, much like the commitment that seals a decisive moment.
desc2:
"The trigger is the most crucial part of any mechanical device. Even from a developer's perspective, I can tell you — no matter how intricate the internal workings are, it's just a piece of scrap if the trigger doesn't function properly. Trust me, I speak from experience — if my trigger had jammed back then, I wouldn't be here today."

— An unnamed veteran traveller

name: Flamme De Epuration: Frame
desc: Crafted with precision from the blueprint of Flamme De Epuration. Sturdy and robust, it doubles effectively as a blunt instrument or a throwable weapon when out of bullets.
desc2:
"Sure, the legion gives us some freedom to customise our weapons, but painting my gun pink? That's where I draw the line! I don't care if you're my sister, that's still a no. And take that teddy bear charm off!"

— Lynn, an officer of the Hyperborean Legion

name: Flamme De Epuration: Barrel
desc: Crafted with precision from the blueprint of Flamme De Epuration. Bullets burst forth from here, as both the barrel and the warrior's heart blaze with unrelenting fervour.
desc2:
"I know everyone here likes to think of themselves as artists, but seriously, you're all a bunch of morons. What you do is simply alchemy, medicine, or drawing. What's the point of obsessing over the meaning of life or the consequences of your work? Check out this new gun I made — awesome, right?"

— Nisaya, Weapon Master of The Aeolipile

name: Gold Sand
desc: A special product from the other side of the desert. It can be crafted into exquisite decorations or used to strengthen components. The final quality depends on how much real sand gets mixed in during transportation—since it is hard to distinguish between the two, deal with trusted merchants if necessary.
desc2:
"Here I lay in eternal repose,
Beneath countless sand grains,
With no opulent sepulchre,
But at dawn's light,
My golden grave gleams bright."

— "The Gold Miners' Evening Bell", a Khemet ballad

name: Creeping Tendrils
desc:
A creeping plant commonly found in shaded areas, highly flexible with intertwined fibers. After processing, they are used in various applications, and they are durable and resistant to wear. 
Said to be the inspiration for cable design.
desc2:
"Also known as the Ashless Wood, dark in colour, with leaves white as bone; resembling rotten timber, yet flame shuns its touch.
Its bark is edible, with an astringent and cold taste, non-toxic.
Can soothe swollen throats and quell inner heat, taken twice daily in a brew."

— Fufeng, Huaxu Apothecary, in "Essentials of Medicinal Herbs"

name: Virifly
desc: A subspecies of butterfly in Atlasia, its verdant hue heralds the arrival of spring.
desc2:
"If only spring at Icelake lasted longer. For most of the year, all we see is endless snow. On days when viriflies aren't around, evergreen plants are the closest thing we have to spring."

— Psyche, an Icelake resident

name: Indigofly
desc: A subspecies of butterfly in Atlasia, its indigo hue is pure and striking.
desc2:
"To think that butterflies can live in the snow — such a miraculous and beautiful form of life. Hidden within the buds of winter plants, they metamorphose and emerge when the flowers bloom, like ethereal blossoms."

— Miller, a botanist of Aethyrie

name: Spring Water
desc: This clear, tasteless spring water is believed to be a divine gift in Elysium, said to cleanse the soul and wash away worldly impurities.
desc2:
"Shed the dust, the weariness, and the noise in your mind. Let it all wash away with the waters, and you'll come to truly know yourself."

— Tal, Unofficial Preacher of Elysian Church

name: Snowcap
desc:
A type of fungus capable of surviving in extreme cold. Its appearance often leads people to mistake it for a pile of unmelted snow. Its toxins can cause hallucinations if ingested, and in severe cases, can be life-threatening.

DO NOT EAT! DO NOT EAT! DO NOT EAT!
desc2:
"A Filthoid and a snowman, boogie...boogie till the end..."

— A victim of Snowcap poisoning

name: Phoxichor Canister
desc: A liquid derived primarily from Phoxene, serving as the most important energy source powering the entire Hyperborean Empire. Its uses extend far beyond what is commonly known.
desc2:
"Phoxichor may be common, but it is far from ordinary — it embodies the distilled genius of imperial alchemists across ages. Personally, I believe it should be reserved for only a select few, to truly underscore its significance."

— An Aeolipile alchemist specializing in material science research

name: Dewiolet
desc: A common flower found across Atlasia, used in medicine.
desc2:
"Clad in royal purple and featuring intricate blue double petals and slender stem, this herb withstands harsh cold.
Direct consumption is cautioned against, as it can chill the heart and limbs.
Cook it at high heat to create a soothing, detoxifying decoction."

— Fufeng, Huaxu Apothecary, in "Essentials of Medicinal Herbs"

name: Seashell
desc: Seashells are washed up on the beach every day, but finding one intact and vibrantly coloured is always a small stroke of luck.
desc2:
"Shells were the only ornaments we could get back then. After the tide went out, we'd search for the prettiest ones to decorate our huts. I still remember the most beautiful one I found — smooth and pure white, shimmering like a rainbow in the sunlight..."

— A resident of Purgatorio Island

name: Eclipta Grass
desc:
This cold-loving freshwater plant is known as the "winter lotus." Its seeds are transparent and as dreamy and fragile as foam.

IT'S TOXIC! HIGHLY TOXIC! EXTREMELY TOXIC!
desc2:
"Please be cautious around unfamiliar wild plants and fungi. Avoid picking, buying, or selling species like Frostungus and Eclipta Grass, commonly known as 'Snowcap' and 'Bubble Bean.'"

— Rhythm Fischer, Garrison Officer of Icelake

name: Portable Power Unit
desc: A compact emergency energy source essential for large-scale facilities. Preloaded with stabilised Phoxichor, the unit remains functional for extended periods. Simply insert it into a machine's designated power slot to activate.
desc2:
"Everyone knows Phoxichor in portable canisters tends to leak over time. Sure, we've optimised the container to minimise that — we really did our best. But if you want a fully sealed casing, the materials alone would cost more than the Phoxichor inside. Don't like it? File a complaint with Materials. But that's not the point. The point is — we told the quartermaster these things expire after two years. Technically, though... they could last three."

"What's your point?"

"The time has come — it's been two years. Anyone fancy grabbing some 'expired' Phoxichor from the Legion depot?"

"...You're a genius! No wonder your lab never files requisitions."

— Anonymous alchemist, overheard at a secret tea party, as collected in Gatherings Under the Night-Blooming Jasmine

name: Crackbloom
desc: A common wildflower with no formal name, known by different nicknames across regions. No one cultivates it on purpose, and few even notice it — but no matter how often it's plucked, it always grows back in droves. Its resilience is nothing short of remarkable.
desc2:
"A nameless bloom. An unloved species. Maybe someone once cherished it — briefly — before casting it aside. Legend claims it was once a person, punished for defying the gods: stripped of name, of love, of all goodness, and every thread of hope for tomorrow. And yet... it still blooms. Everywhere. Flowers do not speak. But it seems even the gods could not truly silence this one."

— Mendir, Master Gardener, Flora, Flow, and Fate

name: Sacral Bellflower
desc: A plant that thrives in the cracks of stone and brick. It favours damp, shaded places, but withstands intense radiation, cold, drought, and poor soil with surprising ease. Some households even scatter Sacral Bellflower seeds along their walls — and by the following year, those same walls will be draped in a lush, living tapestry of natural ornamentation.
desc2:
"The Sacral Bellflower always droops its head. Shaped like tiny trumpets, it's neither rare nor hard to grow. In Elysium, it symbolises humility, and is said to be a messenger of the divine — delicately whispering sacred teachings to all beings. It's believed that if you listen beneath its blooms for a full day and night, you may earn the blessing of the Great Nine. That said, I wouldn't recommend trying it — the pollen clings to your clothes and is nearly impossible to wash out."

— Mendir, Master Gardener, Flora, Flow, and Fate

name: Bird Egg
desc: Commonly found in areas with dense tree cover. In some remote regions, bird eggs are a popular breakfast item. Just don't go stealing any from the nests near your home — if the mother bird catches you, your windows may never be clean again.
desc2:
"SKREEEEE!!!!!!"

— An enraged mother bird, mid-peck at an egg thief

name: Caramellus
desc: An edible fungus known for its savoury taste and widespread presence across the continent. Nearly every culture has its own unique way of preparing it.
desc2:
"In Hyperborea, pickled mushrooms are the most cherished side dish during the long winters. In Huaxu, people of all ages head into the mountains after rain to forage for them. In Luca, meat-sauce coil pasta and creamy mushroom ribbon pasta are practically half our national faith — (the other half, according to a colleague of mine, being pizza without fruit). In Elysian families, no gathering is complete without a plump mushroom pie. And in Aethyrie, mushroom cake is said to spark inspiration — always sold out come exam season. We travelled the continent in search of good food, but what we found far exceeded our expectations."

— Wym, food journalist from Luca, A Taste of Atlasia

name: Skylily
desc: The most common and vital flower of Huaxu. In bloom, its exotic fragrance fills the air — a primary source for Huaxu's incense. It is these delicate, easily-broken plants that became the very force sustaining the Nine Chapters of Dafeng.
desc2:
"This is the first herb I recorded in Essentials of Medicinal Herbs. Skylily has little medicinal value, but its significance is undeniable. People always mock what I do, yet everyone enjoys the benefits of herbs. Such stubborn minds. If people can extract incense from plants to honour the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, shouldn't using them to heal and save lives be just as simple?"

— Notes of the Physician Fufeng

name: Waywardstone
desc: A product of the Scourge of Zhuyin. This crystal inhibits the growth of flora within its area, causing the local ecosystem to stagnate. Due to this unreasonable nature, it is called "Waywardstone".
desc2:
"'My heart's no Waywardstone, yet cannot turn.
 A dye may fade; with this, no return.'

Note: I learned not long ago that my understanding of this popular ballad was slightly off — 'Waywardstone' is actually a specific kind of stone. And the line means: My resolve, like the Waywardstone, cannot be reversed. What is dyed may still fade in time, but once touched by the Waywardstone, it remains unchanged even after years."

— Wangchun, Secretary to Zhiliu, "Index of Common Dyes"

name: Broken Relic
desc: Broken weapons, common on Crowsong Hollow, have drifted with the rivers to Haze Market. They are silent witnesses to the grim history between Xuanheng Sect and Jishu Sect. If these relics could speak, and tell truthfully all they have seen and heard, perhaps Huaxu would be a different place today.
desc2:
"Sometimes the truth of history is nothing but an impenetrable fog. To this day, there is no account of the upheaval that decided Huaxu's fate that satisfies everyone. Some in Huaxu believe Heaven had its own design — and according to that design, the Xuanheng Sect succeeded in carrying out a series of actions against the Jishu Sect, ultimately banishing Zhuyin and emerging as the final victor of the turmoil. Since then, the Argent Loong Taihao alone has served as the 'voice of Heaven,' ruling Huaxu for a thousand years."

— Tachitus, Elysium historian, "Chronicles"

name: Loomhopper
desc: An insect commonly found in Huaxu, said to chirp like the sound of a weaving loom, hence its name. It changes color with its surroundings, and hunting for it among summer grasses is a favorite pastime for children.
desc2:
"We used to play this with our junior brother: light a stick of incense and see who could catch more Loomhoppers. Kezhou was so noisy he scared away more than he caught. As the senior brother, I had to let them win. Buxia, with her sharp ears, always took first place."

— Yuming, Huaxu Magistrate of Yingtian

name: Skink
desc: Also known as Earth Loong, it loves basking on sun-warmed stones but is remarkably alert. The moment it senses vibrations through the rock, it vanishes into hidden crevices. Some keep them as pets, and their strikingly blue tails are said to have a surprisingly pleasing texture.
desc2:
Skink on the rock,
Gone with the sound.
Stare till you drop—
Just its tail, waggling around.

— A doggerel from Haze Market

name: Rainseer Frog
desc: A frog that perpetually stares straight at the sky, as if communing with the heavens. Experienced farmers know that once the Rainseer Frog begins to call incessantly, a rain shower is approaching, and it's time to bring the drying grains indoors.
desc2:
The Rainseer Frog sings only when layered clouds gather like ink, hence the elders call it the "Cloud-Drawn Messenger." This holds especially true from the Summer Solstice until the End of Heat, when the vital breaths of heaven and earth converge.

— The Essential Art of Farming

name: Gritfly
desc: Once a common Virifly found everywhere. But just as the Gritblight Expanse were once a vibrant green land, the Scourge of Zhuyin has gradually stained all things here with stagnation, turning them an ominous black-purple.
desc2:
"Life adapts — whether to bitter cold or scorching lava. Even the super-natural environment of eastern Huaxu, tainted by Zhuyin, is not entirely devoid of vitality. The emergence of the Gritfly stands as yet another testament to this truth."

— Notes from a Hyperborean biologist

name: Ironshell Nut
desc: Sizable brown nuts, also edible — if one can crack their rock-hard shell like a rodent.
desc2:
"Squeak, squeak, squeak, squeak, squeak..."

— A foraging squirrel trying to crack an Ironshell Nut

name: Goldshell Nut
desc: A rarer variant of Ironshell Nuts, also edible. They are richer in oil content than the common variety. When roasted, they burst open, making them a popular snack among kids.
desc2:
"Squeak, squeak, squeak, squeak, squeak... SQUEAK!!!"

— A foraging squirrel that has just cracked an Goldshell Nut

name: Silverite
desc: A silvery mineral with a metallic lustre that ranges from black to silver depending on its purity.
desc2:
"Work hard today, live in comfort for the rest of your days!" 

— Motivational sign in the Silverite mine

name: Lumite
desc: A rarer variant of Silverite, mixed with impurities that unexpectedly enhance its lustre.
desc2:
"Work hard today, live in comfort for the rest of your days! 

Note: Unauthorised possession of Silverite and Lumite is a capital offence."

— Updated motivational sign in the Silverite mine

name: Plop Plop Stone
desc: With a scientific name "Lakestone," this stone is commonly known as the "Plop Plop Stone" due to its widespread use in stone-skipping games. The number of "plops" made across the water is crucial in determining who gets to be an aspiring leader among the local kids.
desc2:
"Troubles to stones, 'plop, plop' as they go, where they're gone from sight, in Lamenting Lake they're beyond." 

— A folk ballad of Icelake

name: Coralstone
desc: White stalactites, known to the people of Huaxu as "Coralstone." Their existence bears witness to untold ages of shifting terrains. When ground and consumed, they can alleviate lung weakness, cough, and general debility — though they do tend to scratch the throat on the way down.
desc2:
"This powder mill is an order from Zesheng Pharmacy. Before I figured this thing out, they had to hire Loongscion to pound hard herbs into dust by hand. But any respectable Loongscion has their own proper trade — most who took the jobs were… questionable sorts. The Hall folks just turned a blind eye... One of them got famous lately, called Ke... Ke-something, wasn't it?"

— Gongshang, Mechanist of Huaxu Jishu Sect

name: Festive Afterglow
desc: Used to heighten the festive ambience during the Festive Gathering event
desc2:
Let go of the troubles beyond your reach.
 Hold fast to the smiles you've shared, and treasure every rare moment spent together.
 Let your body relax, let your laughter rise, and let this once-a-year celebration carry you away.

name: Unbreakable Hammer
desc: A forging hammer supplied by Lunosmith, powerful enough to work almost any material into shape. Used to heighten the festive ambience during the Festive Gathering event.
desc2: "I heard the theatre's crafting a special backdrop for Snow — fine idea, that. So I lent them my hammer. And you're asking why a ball needs a hammer? Hah. My hammer doesn't just forge weapons — it's perfect for shaping stage props as well."

name: Scented Candles
desc: Banquet candles supplied by Lunotress, creating a warm, cosy ambience wherever they're placed. Used to heighten the festive ambience during the Festive Gathering event.
desc2: "A good dance needs the right atmosphere — music, a stage, and proper lighting. You know the first two better than I do, so... take these candles. Warm light, gentle glow. The scent might make people a bit sleepy, but if everyone's busy dancing... it should be fine."

name: Doomsday Survival Kit
desc: A survival kit assembled by Lunogloom, stocked with thirty days' worth of canned food, potable water, and basic sewing supplies. Used to heighten the festive ambience during the Festive Gathering event.
desc2: "The end is nigh... just as it was yesterday, and the day before. Yet here you are — singing, dancing, as if nothing could trouble you. It's... unsettling. So I've put together some supplies. If the world ends without warning, at least you'll have what you need to keep on dancing."

name: "Stylish" Decor Trinkets
desc: A bundle of "stylish" trinkets offered by Lunoxplorer. They make surprisingly effective decor — though on closer inspection, they're really just stones, shells, and leaves she gathered on her travels. Used to heighten the festive ambience during the Festive Gathering event.
desc2: "A theatre's not really my place. Explorers belong to mountains and oceans, not gilded domes. Still, your decor could use a touch of the wild. So take these — shells from the coast, pebbles from Lamenting Lake, and leaves from Aethyrie. They'll give your stage a bit of proper outdoor charm."

name: Huaxu Crimson Silk
desc: Crimson silk from Huaxu supplied by an invited Starweaver Luno — smooth, lustrous, and a rare sight in Icelake. Used to heighten the festive ambience during the Festive Gathering event.
desc2: "Hyperborea is so far away and so cold! People there must wrap up in fur or padded coats... they probably never see silk at all. So I thought — why not send some for the stage decor? And who knows — maybe it'll even bring a few customers to my stall! Hopefully!"

name: Tidewanderer
desc: A key commercial species across Atlasia, this fish can be found in every sea. It forms vast schools in the open ocean and migrates to coastal shallows with the turning of the seasons, year after year.
desc2:
Tidewanderers follow the seasons like clockwork, setting off on their great migration the same month each year, no matter how rough the seas. In honour of their uncanny punctuality — and to better profit from it — coastal folk began forging clock hands in the shape of a Tidewanderer.

— Dylan the Know-It-All, Unknown Corners

name: Tidewanderer Variant
desc: A key commercial species across Atlasia, this fish can be found in every sea. It forms vast schools in the open ocean and migrates to coastal shallows with the turning of the seasons, year after year.
desc2:

— Dylan the Know-It-All, Unknown Corners

name: Prismspike
desc: A brilliantly coloured fish found in crystal-clear waters, easily recognised by the vivid spines along its back. Skittish by nature — when fishing, patience serves better than speed.
desc2:
Back in the day, its gaudy colours and spiny back had fishermen mistaking it for something venomous. Most just dried it out and sold it as a decorative specimen. Then some brave soul with more guts than sense gave it a try — and before long, Prismspikes started gracing dinner tables across the continent. As for those flashy spines? Just another kind of unrecyclable waste.

— Fiama, designer, Refractions

name: Silverslip
desc: A slender marine fish that swims upright, its scales gleaming like liquid silver in motion — true to its name. Unfortunately, it perishes quickly once removed from the water, and due to the high cost of transport, it is seldom seen on inland tables.
desc2:
In every seaside town, you'll find Silverslip on the New Year's table. In some regions, there's a tradition of hiding a silver coin in the fish's belly — and whoever finds it is said to enjoy good fortune all year long.

— Dylan the Know-It-All, Unknown Corners

name: Longwhisker
desc: Named for the long barbels near its mouth, this freshwater species dwells in muddy beds thick with waterweed. It only surfaces after sundown to feed and can live for decades — if it avoids the hook.
desc2:
Its diet is so absurdly varied that parents in fishing villages often use it to teach their kids a life lesson: "A long life starts with an empty plate."

— Dylan the Know-It-All, Unknown Corners

desc: Named for the long barbels near its mouth, this freshwater species dwells in muddy beds thick with waterweed. It only surfaces after sundown to feed and can live for decades — if it avoids the hook.

name: Spotted Tagalong
desc: Densely covered in pearl-like spots, this fish can grow up to two metres long. The young are gentle by nature and rarely stray far from their parents' tailfins.
desc2:
Not the brightest type of fish, honestly. Fry often mistake other large fish for their parents. With the right technique, you could have one trailing behind you for quite a while — just be careful not to get bitten when the real parents show up.

— Harriet, nature writer, World Beneath the Waves

desc: Densely covered in pearl-like spots, this fish can grow up to two metres long. The young are gentle by nature and rarely stray far from their parents' tailfins.

name: Shellgnarl
desc: Found throughout freshwater bodies, the Shellgnarl is one of the few ingredients beloved by nearly every community on the continent. Preparation methods vary by region — some even throw grand summer festivals featuring it as the star dish.
desc2:
Tired of scrubbing shellgnarls one by one? Ditch your old brush and gloves — and say hello to the Pull & Spin Shellgnarl Washer™! Bulk cleaning made easy — no fuss, no scraped knuckles. Comes in two sizes: a handy 1-litre model for home use, and a 10-litre industrial beast!

— A poster outside a general store

name: Shellgnarl Variant
desc: Found throughout freshwater bodies, the Shellgnarl is one of the few ingredients beloved by nearly every community on the continent. Preparation methods vary by region — some even throw grand summer festivals featuring it as the star dish.

— A poster outside a general store

name: Fangnome
desc: With its sharp fangs and perpetually scowling face, this fish looks far more dangerous than it actually is. The largest one ever recorded measured just 5 centimetres. It doesn't hunt in packs, and its bite is harmless — at most leaving a faint, circular scar.
desc2:
"According to workplace safety regulations, a Fangnome bite doesn't count as an occupational injury. I'm afraid I can't approve your sick leave."

— Burt, supervisor of Icelake Urban Maintenance Office

name: Fangnome Variant
desc: With its sharp fangs and perpetually scowling face, this fish looks far more dangerous than it actually is. The largest one ever recorded measured just 5 centimetres. It doesn't hunt in packs, and its bite is harmless — at most leaving a faint, circular scar.
desc2:

— Burt, supervisor of Icelake Urban Maintenance Office

name: Nomnom
desc: A near-motionless fish that spends most of its life lying sideways in the silt. With its mouth perpetually agape, it waits for plankton and small fish to drift in. Once it bites, it chews for hours without so much as a twitch — a habit that gave it its name.
desc2:
"A thoroughly unappetising species — both to us and to other fish. I once saw a Bonegnaw Eel take a bite and spit it out straight away, like it was saying 'yuck' — which is a rare reaction for a fish, mind you.
The Nomnom was fine, physically speaking — but then it just floated up, belly-first, nice and slow. Yes, it literally scared to death."

— Harriet, nature writer, World Beneath the Waves

name: Mr Leggy
desc: A bizarre creature that looks like a crab crossed with a spider. It scuttles up walls like the latter and haunts the depths like the former. While there are many ways to catch one, angling remains by far the safest.
desc2:
"I've got a Mr Leggy trapped under a bucket. Now... how do I get it out of the house without lifting the bucket?"

"...! Ahem. Old Martin, I'm staying at Ms Camilla's tonight. Don't wait up."

— A conversation between a daughter and her father

name: Guiding Star
desc: A tiny jellyfish found only in the waters around Purgatorio Island, known for its bioluminescence. Though inedible, its glow lights the waves on moonless nights — bobbing like a star set adrift, guiding fishermen home.
desc2:
Back on Purgatorio Island, we called it the "Guiding Star." They say its glow lasts forever as long as you care for it — much like a star forever shining in the sky. My father caught this one the day I was born. The years have blurred so much, but not this. It's still there — glowing, steadfast, right where my story began.

— Abigail Morley, a seafood trader in Luca

— Abigail Morley, a seafood trader in Luca

name: Tidechaser
desc: One of the primary catches for villagers on Purgatorio Island, prized for its tender, flavourful flesh — the result of a life spent in constant motion, ceaselessly chasing the ebb and flow of the tides.
desc2:
Fresh Tidechaser is best eaten raw. The taste doesn't just hit your tongue — it shoots straight from your teeth to your brain. In that moment, you feel the flick of its tail, the ocean parting in its wake. And most who are lucky enough to try it, without fail, say the same thing: "You can really taste the life in it!"

— Ethans, food critic, Eat It, Love It, Know It

name: Seaskimmer
desc: Native to Purgatorio Island, this species can glide across the water's surface. On clear days, you might spot them leaping into the air like birds — their vibrant wings shimmering in the sun.
desc2:
Chasing freedom means taking risks.

Just look at it — born a fish, but dreaming of the sky. For one fleeting moment, it tastes freedom... And the next? Snatched midair by a seabird for lunch.

— A Purgatorio Island parent, mid-lesson

name: Seapuff
desc: The most beloved aquatic creature on Purgatorio Island, with no recorded counterpart elsewhere. Plainly inedible, these fairy-like beings bring a spark of delight to islanders living far from the outside world, easing the monotony of their isolated days.
desc2:
Yes, yes — I know I should've given it a more taxonomically accurate name. But come on — who could call this adorable little thing a "shell-less snail"? I mean, just look at it! A puffy little bundle of joy, right!?

Hmm... puffy... puff... sea... Seapuff. Yes. That's the one.

— A passionately insistent marine biologist

name: Silverfrond
desc: A rare and exceptionally beautiful fish, its fins shimmer like the gleaming boughs of a Heaventree. On Purgatorio Island, it is revered as a gift from the divine — and when caught, it is often returned to the sea in quiet reverence.
desc2:
A captive soul, long steeped in weary gloom,
Needs no hard hand to tumble into doom.
The sea, though dark, would make a fitting grave —
Yet divine light bloomed beneath the deepest wave.

The sundered boughs of Heaventree were wings,
Their leaf-born hymns, the veil that grace brings.
Through depths unknown, I heard Their distant call,
And felt my shattered form rise — not to fall —
...but back towards life once more.

— Excerpt from The Saga of Torrential Grudges, by Alexander Dumas, a mourning faction playwright

name: Pearldrop Flatfin
desc: A speciality of the Huaxu Waters, often dubbed the "bat of the sea" by locals. It typically dwells near the seabed, surfacing only to feed. Its back is studded with pearlescent bumps — a texture prized for wrapping the hilts of fine weapons.
desc2:
The beast towered over twenty feet tall — fanged, clawed, steeped in bloodlust. In the blink of an eye, it struck again. But the Yingtian Marshal had already moved. Not a word. Not a breath. The blade rose — then fell. A clean arc cleaved through the creature's snarling face.

What a blade! Thus lauds the verse:

With Pearldrop hide the hilt is bound, firm in his hand.
Forged by master smiths, the blade he doth command.
Heaven-blest, sworn to repay, he makes a solemn vow:
For the Argent Dragon's honour due, thy head must fall ere now.

— Excerpt from Chronicles of Yingtian, a Huaxu storytelling classic

name: Gearshell Crab
desc: A crab that makes its home inside abandoned clockwork parts. Though biologically little different from ordinary hermit crabs, the collapse of the Jishu Sect left behind scattered mechanical relics — now repurposed by these creatures as shelters across the seas.
desc2:
We still don't know how this species developed such particular taste in housing — but picture this: hundreds of metal casings, each sprouting jointed limbs, scuttling across the beach in swarms... Burned into my memory, no doubt. Though it would've been nicer if they hadn't tried to pinch my toes.

— An anonymous veteran explorer

name: Pearllure
desc: A mysterious aquatic lifeform recorded in ancient texts, said to spit venomous sand at the shadows of passers-by, afflicting them with strange illnesses.
desc2:
Though this species does eject sand in short bursts, it bears little resemblance to the mythical creature "Yuu" described in early Huaxu writings. 
The expelled sand is demonstrably non-toxic, and the naming may well be a case of ancestral misattribution — or simple mythological conflation. Most likely, the original "Yuu" never existed at all.

— Lin Caocao, biologist from Huaxu

name: Yuu
desc: A fiercely aggressive species prized for its tender, flavourful meat — a familiar sight on dining tables across Huaxu. Despite its hideous appearance, the bioluminescent lure atop its head lends it a strangely delicate beauty.
desc2:
In ancient times, fishermen believed that the Pearllure's glowing lure was none other than the fabled Night Pearl itself. But once the creature perished, its radiance faded swiftly — and thus arose the old Huaxu proverb: "The bright pearl dims when cast astray."

— Rovetta, travel writer, Rovetta in Huaxu

name: Twincrest Shark
desc: Named after the once-popular twin-bun hairstyle of Huaxu, this swift and ferocious predator is an opportunistic feeder, known for tearing through nets with ease — a true challenge for even seasoned fishers.
desc2:
Twincrest Sharks have eyes that diverge, never quite meeting in focus. In their long-standing feud, the Jishu and Xuanheng sects seized even this quirk as fuel for mockery. The Jishu jeered that the Xuanheng "saw no one but themselves," so blind were they with pride. The Xuanheng retorted that the Jishu, like flatfish, were "short-sighted to the point of absurdity."
Unknowing is the creature — yet in human hands, its name becomes a blade.

— Lin Caocao, biologist from Huaxu

name: Phoxenetrout
desc: A fish bearing a striking resemblance to Phoxene, with an uncanny texture that feels almost indistinguishable from the real thing. No two look quite the same — but they all share one unfortunate trait: flesh as tough as stone. It's rarely eaten except in times of true desperation.
desc2:
Toothache keeping you up? Go catch a Phoxene. Boil it — not that it'll help. Then bite down hard. That bad tooth of yours? Pop — gone on its own. Works every time.

— Icelake's Tooth-Pulling Trick (Guaranteed to Hurt)

name: Lady of the Lake
desc: A brilliantly coloured fish that glides through the water like a wisp of silk. Its translucent fins ripple around it like trailing veils, and every motion flows with effortless poise — graceful as the fabled Lady of the Lake, wandering her liquid realm in quiet command.
desc2:
The Lady of the Lake is far more dangerous than her beauty suggests. Even while on the hunt, it moves with breathtaking poise. One "kiss" — and even prey several times her size falls limp. Strangely, it is never been known to harm a human. In fact, it has even been spotted sharing its surplus catch with fishermen from time to time.

— Harriet, nature writer, World Beneath the Waves

name: Lamenting Lake Trout
desc: One of the staple food fish in Icelake, easily recognised by the single horn atop its head. Large, tender, and low in bones, it suits sashimi, grilling, frying, or baking — a truly versatile catch for any dish.
desc2:
This fish died twice — once in the kitchen, and once more on the plate. I've had bad fish before, but this? Easily a new number one. Off the table. Start over.

— Ethans, food critic, judging at a cooking competition

name: Washer's Club
desc: A rare, cold-hardy fish found only in Icelake. With a tough, ridged carapace and no dorsal or ventral fins, it is easy to grip, much like the wooden clubs once used to pound laundry clean.
desc2:
Technically, it has a long-winded academic name — but most people still prefer the nickname given by a washerwoman over the official term coined by biologists.

— Dylan the Know-It-All, Unknown Corners

name: Gleamspine
desc: A species unique to the waters of Icelake. Jagged, ice-like spines line its back, glowing faintly in the dark. On clear days, a streak of pale light beneath the surface often signals the silent passing of a Gleamspine.
desc2:
I watched it go — one scar at a time, it shed the past. It had grown strong, outgrown the bounds of the bathtub. And for the first time, it swam free — its glowing spine tracing a ray of light across the open sea.

— Consul, novelist, Gleamspine in the Sewers

name: Iridescentscale
desc: A vibrant, frilled fish prized for its looks. The fuller the fins, the brighter the colours, the higher the price. Fiercely territorial toward its own kind, each must be housed alone.
desc2:
In dazzling hues, it weaves through tide,
Iridescent scales in ripples glide.
In solitude — a beauty unmatched, serene.
In pairs — all grace gives way to spite unseen.

— Nameless poet, Ode to the Iridescentscale
